source.title: Anthropometric and fitness profile of high-level basketball, handball and volleyball players

paper.citation: Peña, J., Moreno-Doutres, D., Coma, J., Cook, M., & Buscà, B. (2018). Anthropometric and fitness profile of high-level basketball, handball and volleyball players. Revista Andaluza de Medicina del Deporte, 11(1), 30–35. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ramd.2016.03.002
paper.abstract: Do anthropometric measures, jump performance, change-of-direction test time, and bench-press power differ among high-level male basketball, handball, and volleyball players? Participants: 46 male Spanish first-division professionals: basketball 18, handball 15, and volleyball 13; mean age 26.1 ± 4.8 years. Sport and level: One professional club from each of three sports; athletes represented 14 countries and 22 had senior national-team experience. Training or return-to-play context: In-season profiling, not an intervention or return-to-play study. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Male professionals only; sport groups were also club groups, and playing-position distributions were not modeled. Design: Cross-sectional descriptive comparison. Exposure or intervention: None. Comparator: Basketball, handball, and volleyball groups. Measurements and outcomes: Height, standing reach, body mass, seven-site skinfold-estimated body fat, squat jump, countermovement jump, countermovement jump with arm swing, 4 × 5 m change-of-direction test, and bench-press power at 20, 40, 60, and 80 kg. Analysis: Three testing sessions; one-way ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis with Holm–Sidak or Dunn post-hoc comparisons at p ≤ 0.05.
paper.tldr: This cross-sport profile informs test-battery interpretation by illustrating how anthropometry and performance-test distributions differ across professional basketball, handball, and volleyball samples. Basketball players were taller and had greater standing reach than the other groups; handball players had higher estimated body fat than basketball and volleyball players. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Cross-sectional descriptive comparison. Exposure or intervention: None. Comparator: Basketball, handball, and volleyball groups. Measurements and outcomes: Height, standing reach, body mass, seven-site skinfold-estimated body fat, squat jump, countermovement jump, countermovement jump with arm swing, 4 × 5 m change-of-direction test, and bench-press power at 20, 40, 60, and 80 kg. Analysis: Three testing sessions; one-way ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis with Holm–Sidak or Dunn post-hoc comparisons at p ≤ 0.05.
paper.findings: Basketball players were taller and had greater standing reach than the other groups; handball players had higher estimated body fat than basketball and volleyball players. Volleyball players performed better in countermovement and arm-swing countermovement jumps, while squat-jump performance did not differ significantly by sport. Basketball players completed the 4 × 5 m test faster than handball and volleyball players, and handball players were faster than volleyball players. At 40 kg, concentric bench-press mean power was 793 ± 68 W in basketball, 629 ± 93 W in handball, and 569 ± 87 W in volleyball, with basketball higher than both groups.
paper.limitations: Each sport was represented by one club, so sport, team selection, coaching, and roster composition were confounded. Small male-only groups and unmodeled positional roles limit generalization. Cross-sectional differences cannot determine whether the observed profile reflects training adaptations, talent selection, body size, or test familiarity. Fixed-load bench-press power favors athletes differently based on strength and body mass, and the 4 × 5 m test represents one constrained change-of-direction task. The authors stated that further work was needed before generalizing the profiles or establishing the age at which differences emerge.
paper.practicalImplications: Use sport and position context when comparing tests, and prefer team- and role-specific longitudinal references over broad cross-sport norms. These distributions may help select a battery, but they should not become talent-selection cutoffs or evidence that one sport's training caused a particular physical profile.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use sport and position context when comparing tests, and prefer team- and role-specific longitudinal references over broad cross-sport norms. These distributions may help select a battery, but they should not become talent-selection cutoffs or evidence that one sport's training caused a particular physical profile. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
